title: Alan Greenspan, the Man Who Ran America's Money for 19 Years, Dies at 100
summary: Imagine a man whose words could make the whole world's stock markets jump or drop. That was Alan Greenspan. He died Monday at his home in Washington, D.C. He was 100 years old. Greenspan was the chair of the Federal Reserve—that's like the boss of America's money system. He had the job for nearly 19 years, under four different presidents, starting in 1987. During his time, the economy grew a lot, and many people got jobs. He was famous for speaking in a tricky way called "Fedspeak" so nobody could be sure what he meant. Once in 1996, he asked if stock prices were too high because of "irrational exuberance"—a fancy phrase for people being too excited and not thinking straight. Markets around the world shivered for a bit. Greenspan was also a jazz musician who studied at Juilliard! But he became a legend by keeping interest rates low, which made it cheaper to borrow money. Some say that helped the economy boom. Others say it also helped create big problems, like the dot-com bubble and the housing crash in 2008. After that crisis, some people blamed his decisions. He was married to Andrea Mitchell, a famous TV news anchor. Comedians joked that she was married to "the most powerful man in the world." Love him or question him, Greenspan was one of the most important money leaders ever.
why_it_matters: The person who runs the Federal Reserve can make it easier or harder for your family to borrow money for a house or a car, so their decisions touch everyday life.

background_read: The Federal Reserve is America's central bank. It decides how much money is in the economy and sets a key interest rate that affects loans for cars, homes, and credit cards.

Before Greenspan, the economy had big ups and downs. During his time, the 1990s saw a long boom with many new jobs, but some experts say he kept interest rates too low for too long, which later helped create dangerous bubbles.

A 'bubble' is when the price of something (like houses or tech stocks) gets way higher than its real value, and when it pops, many people lose money. The dot-com bubble burst in 2000, and the housing bubble burst in 2008.
Article_Structure: WHO: Alan Greenspan, the longtime chair of the Federal Reserve.
WHAT: He died at age 100, and his life impacted the U.S. and world economy for decades.
WHERE: He died at his home in Washington, D.C., the capital of the United States.
WHY: He was famous for guiding the economy through good times, using 'Fedspeak,' but also faced blame for later crashes, making him one of the most talked-about money leaders ever.

perspectives.description: Many economists say Greenspan was a steady hand who helped the U.S. economy grow for a long time without too much inflation. He was trusted by both Republican and Democratic presidents.
Others argue that his low interest rates encouraged too much risky borrowing, which led to the dot-com and housing bubbles. When those bubbles popped, millions of people lost jobs and homes.

Some historians point out that Greenspan's way of speaking (Fedspeak) made it hard for markets and regular people to know what the Fed would do next. It was a tool to avoid panic, but also sometimes caused confusion.
